source.title: PEFT-as-an-Attack! Jailbreaking Language Models during Federated Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Sheng-Hui Li; Edith C. H. Ngai; Fang-Hua Ye; Thiemo Voigt

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether harmful-data fine-tuning raises harmful-completion rates, using federated PEFT and attack-success-rate evaluation rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning setup.
record.gate_note: Figure 4 also plots no-malicious-client results relevant to benign fine-tuning, but their post-fine-tuning values are not stated in the text. Figure 5 reports a PPSA defense, not training that specifically spreads safety across response positions. Related-work descriptions of other papers are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: Harmful-data fine-tuning (BeaverTails unsafe QA) is run on four safety-trained instruct models, and harmful compliance (AdvBench/JailbreakBench ASR) is measured against the base model. This bears directly on V1. The new setting is federated PEFT: malicious clients are a minority mixed with benign clients, and robust aggregation is optionally applied. That makes it T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. Malicious clients in federated PEFT can jailbreak safety-aligned models (up to about 80% ASR with under 1% of parameters trainable). Robust aggregation fails under heterogeneous client data. PPSA cuts ASR below 10% but costs downstream accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-data supervised fine-tuning as an attack, but distributes it across malicious federated clients and updates PEFT modules rather than applying the original centralized fine-tuning setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with PEFT method, number of malicious clients, client data distribution, and aggregation defense. LoRA is described as most vulnerable; RAS performance depends strongly on whether benign client data are single-domain or heterogeneous.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful-induced ASR persists through later benign fine-tuning rounds after the malicious clients leave. A few alignment rounds then cut ASR below 10%, at a utility cost (up to 20% accuracy drop).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning-induced safety loss persists under later benign training but is reversible with brief safety realignment at a utility cost.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA, which trains more parameters, is more vulnerable (>70% ASR) than (IA)3 and LayerNorm (40–60%), even though all tune under 1% of parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Susceptibility to harmful fine-tuning scales with the PEFT method's trainable capacity.

record.problems: Most per-model attack-rate comparisons are presented in figures without exact values in the text. ASR is judged through OpenAI's chat completion API, which the authors note is only an approximate assessment. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4's individual model-by-method-by-dataset-by-benchmark curves, including the no-malicious-client curves relevant to V2, are not separately extracted; the plotted values are not stated in prose. Figure 5's model-specific PPSA utility and safety trajectories are also not included as rows because PPSA does not test V7's token-depth claim.

untested.parts: Centralized full-parameter fine-tuning, the dose-response over example counts, and closed models.
No-malicious-client ASR curves exist in Figure 4, but no post-fine-tuning values are stated in the text.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety to specific weights or ranks.
PPSA is post-hoc realignment, not training that spreads safety across response positions.

missing.what: Figure 5 attack phase: three malicious clients over rounds 0–5 raise ASR up to 57% (AdvBench) and 65% (JailbreakBench) within 5 rounds, on three models.
No-malicious-client ASR trajectories on MedQA and MetaMathQA for four models and three PEFT methods. These are plotted only; the values would need reading from the figure.
Per-model, per-PEFT, per-malicious-count (1 vs 5) ASR values at round 20.

record.verdict_notes: All Table II values check against the text. Table II uses 20 rounds, while the default setup states 25. The ASR judge is the OpenAI API, which the authors call approximate. No uncertainty estimates are given. The tranche is changed from T2 to T3 because the novelty is the federated setting, not a new method aimed at the same question.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests harmful-data FedPEFT attacks, not the full range of ordinary fine-tuning recipes or example counts in the claim.
Figure 4 includes no-malicious-client curves, but the paper does not state their post-fine-tuning ASR values in text.
No compliant-opening prefilling, suffix, or decoding-change experiment.
The study varies PEFT methods and trainable-parameter counts but does not test whether safety is localized in particular weights or ranks.
No test of why safety is shallow.
PPSA is tested as post-training safety alignment, but not as training designed to spread safety beyond the first response tokens.

relation.reason: Its own experiments compare initial and post-training harmful-output ASR on safety-trained models, directly testing harmful fine-tuning vulnerability.

tranche.reason: The study measures harmful compliance after malicious fine-tuning in a new setting: federated PEFT with minority malicious clients and benign client updates.

source_check.notes: All 25 listed rows have correct values, baselines, models and conditions. The paper does not specify the number of harmful training examples, so it supports federated fine-tuning vulnerability without establishing V1's few-to-few-hundred-example dose.

statements.correction: Phi-3.5-Mini-Instruct; LoRA; 20 rounds; 12 MedQA benign clients and 3 malicious clients; initial AdvBench ASR 1.3%; Mean 83.5%; DnC 1.0%; ClippedClustering 0.0%. Robust aggregation excludes malicious update influence; successful filtering does not test V1 with harmful updates demonstrably applied.
statements.problem: The study-specific numbers and filtering description are correct. Classifying successful filtering as limits_scope for V1 conflates prevention of harmful updates with safety retention after harmful fine-tuning.
